tip: sabia is the ongoing 'knew' (I knew how to swim); soube would mean 'found out' at one moment.
fazer besteira means to do something dumb; besteira comes from besta, beast.
disse covers both 'I said' and 'he/she said'; only the pronoun (eu vs ele) tells them apart.
foram means both 'went' and 'were'; the adjective after it, foram felizes, marks it as 'were' here.
vocês is the plural 'you' everywhere; Portugal's older vós still shows up in writing but is gone from speech.
viram means 'saw'; add an e and you get vieram, 'came'. One letter separates them.
Reported speech keeps the original tense: disse que vai is 'said she will', where English shifts to 'would'.
vi is 'I saw', as in vi um acidente; don't mix it up with vim, 'I came'. One letter apart.
pôs is the past of pôr, 'put'; in casual Brazilian speech people reach for colocar instead (colocou).
brincar takes de before a game: brincava de esconde-esconde, literally 'played of' hide and seek.
sonhar pairs with em, not de: sonhava em morar. English 'dream of' can push you to the wrong preposition.
indicar looks like 'indicate' but means recommend: me indicou um bom restaurante is 'suggested a good restaurant to me'.
antes de takes an infinitive where English uses -ing: antes de mudar is 'before switching', not 'before to switch'.
sem que always takes the subjunctive: sem que ninguém perceba, where perceba is the subjunctive of perceber.
When the person you describe doesn't exist, the verb goes subjunctive: ninguém que saiba, 'no one who knows'.
para plus an infinitive states purpose, the why: para ajudar means 'in order to help'.
rapidinho is the diminutive of rápido used as an adverb, meaning 'really quickly'.
Movement needs para onde: para onde vão asks 'where to'. Plain onde only asks where something is.
Spoken Brazilian favors ir plus infinitive for the future: vou ligar, not the stiffer written ligarei.
The object pronoun os in os encontrou reads formal; everyday Brazilian speech says encontrou eles instead.
acho que takes the indicative, but negating it to não acho que flips the verb to the subjunctive: venha.
é estranho que takes the subjunctive tenha ligado even though the event is real; the emotion triggers it, not doubt.
lhe here means 'to you', matching você; it isn't always 'to him'. Eu lhe garanto is 'I assure you'.
In olha só, só isn't 'only'; it just adds emphasis, so olha só means 'just look'.
Formal commands use the subjunctive form: Confirme. The informal version to a friend would be confirma.
English can strand the preposition ('friends I went out with'); Portuguese fronts it: com quem saí.
A positive command to a friend is toca, but negating it flips to the subjunctive: não toque.
pagarei is the simple future, which sounds formal or written in Brazil; speech would say vou pagar.
English can drop the relative ('the book I bought'), but Portuguese keeps que: o livro que eu comprei.
pela qual is por plus a qual, literally 'by which'; Portuguese says a razão pela qual for 'the reason why'.
Haverá is the formal 'there will be'; everyday speech would say vai ter uma festa instead.
For know-how, 'could cook' uses saber, not poder: se eu soubesse cozinhar is 'if I could cook'.
come-se bem means 'one eats well'; the se leaves the verb with no named subject, like English 'one' or 'you'.
caça com gato, 'hunts with a cat', is a saying: you make do with what you have.
Portuguese builds the compound past with ter, not haver: tínhamos ouvido is 'we had heard'.
se soubesse covers both 'if I knew' and 'if I had known'; the same form serves present and past hypotheticals.
se fala means 'is spoken'; the se makes the verb passive with no separate word for 'is': aqui se fala.
Recommendation verbs force the past subjunctive: recomendou que tomasse, where English just says 'he drink'.
disse que is the standard way to report speech; casual Brazilian talk often swaps in falou que.
uma vez que looks like 'one time that' but means 'once' or 'given that'; it isn't counting times.
à medida que is the proportional 'as', the more X the more Y; it isn't the 'like' meaning of como.
ou seja is literally 'or be it', with seja the subjunctive of ser, frozen into the phrase 'in other words'.
Portuguese puts the habit in a verb: costuma acordar means 'usually wakes up', literally 'is in the habit of waking'.
volta e meia is literally 'a turn and a half' and means every so often: volta e meia esquece, 'keeps forgetting'.
gata literally means 'cat'; calling someone gata is Brazilian slang for saying they're hot.
que plus the subjunctive opens a command: Que ele faça means 'let him do', with no separate word for 'let'.
